Latest Update: Scientists discover a hidden messaging system deep inside the brain

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1052 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Deep within the brainstem is a tiny group of nerve cells that plays an outsized role in how the brain functions.
  • In a recent development, scientists have long assumed that the LC operates like a loudspeaker, sending essentially the same norepinephrine signal across the brain.
  • A Hidden Brain Network That Sends Precise Messages.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deep within the brainstem is a tiny group of nerve cells that plays an outsized role in how the brain functions. This region, called the locus coeruleus (LC), gets its name from the Latin words for "blue place." Although it contains only a small fraction of the brain's neurons, it produces norepinephrine (NE), a chemical messenger that helps regulate attention, learning, heart rate, and the body's reactions to stress and excitement.

In a recent development, scientists have long assumed that the LC operates like a loudspeaker, sending essentially the same norepinephrine signal across the brain. However, a fresh study published in Nature challenges that understanding. Using brain imaging, recordings of neural activity, genetic techniques, and behavioral experiments in mice, researchers at the Allen Institute discovered that the LC communicates through several distinct pathways. Rather than broadcasting one general message, it delivers signals to specific destinations, with different groups of neurons responding to different experiences.

A Hidden Brain Network That Sends Precise Messages.

In a recent development, by tracing the connections of LC neurons, researchers found that different groups of cells communicate with specific regions of the nervous system. These pathways determine where signals trigger the release of norepinephrine, creating a much more organized communication network than previously recognized.

Recent findings suggest that neurons in the upper (dorsal) portion of the LC primarily connect to the cerebral cortex and forebrain. Meanwhile, cells in the lower (ventral) portion send their signals mainly to the brainstem and spinal cord. This arrangement allows different parts of the LC to influence separate brain functions.

"The findings suggest the brain's norepinephrine system is far more like a targeted postal network than a foghorn," stated Karel Svoboda, director of Neural Dynamics at the Allen Institute and study co-author.

Why the Discovery Could Matter for Brain Disorders.

Understanding how this signaling network is organized could eventually change how certain neurological and mental health conditions are treated.

Sources indicate that norepinephrine plays a central role in regulating attention and mood, making it an notable target for medications used to treat depression, anxiety, and ADHD. Neurons in the LC are also among the earliest brain cells to deteriorate in Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that the new findings could have implications for understanding and treating these conditions.

Current treatments that influence norepinephrine can affect multiple brain circuits at once, sometimes producing beneficial effects in one region while causing unwanted effects elsewhere. A clearer map of the LC's specialized pathways could help scientists develop therapies that act more selectively on the circuits involved in particular symptoms.

The research received support from the National Institutes of Health's Brain Research Through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies® Initiative, also known as The BRAIN Initiative®.

Scientists Identify Brain Cells Involved in Learning.

The researchers also uncovered an important distinction between the functions of different LC neurons.

Cells in the dorsal LC that connect to the cortex were particularly active during learning. When mice performed decision-making tasks and adjusted their choices after an unfavorable result, these neurons increased their activity.

Neurons in the ventral LC behaved differently. Their activity rose shortly before mice ignored signals indicating that a reward might be available. This suggests that these cells help regulate whether animals respond to opportunities in their surroundings.

According to recent reports, "What emerged was a clear map: neurons in the dorsal LC that send signals upward to the cortex are involved in learning, whereas neurons in the ventral region projecting downward to the brainstem and spinal cord govern whether animals engage with their environment at all," remarked Svoboda. "We also revealed that these anatomical differences are mirrored by distinct gene expression patterns.".

These findings indicate that the differences between the two groups extend beyond their locations and connections. They also have distinct patterns of gene activity that reflect their specialized roles.

Researchers Discover a Record-Breaking Neuron.

The study involved an extensive examination of the mouse brain. Scientists used whole-brain imaging to study nearly 35,000 neurons, analyzed the genetic profiles of almost 400,000 cells, and reconstructed the complete structures of several exceptionally complex nerve cells.

Recent findings suggest that during this work, they encountered another remarkable finding: LC neurons possess extraordinarily long axons. These projections carry signals from nerve cells to other cells, allowing information to travel across the nervous system.

Industry observers note that the researchers found that LC axons measured approximately 35 centimeters long on average. One particularly extraordinary axon had a total reconstructed length of 70.32 centimeters, making it part of the longest single neuron ever measured in a mouse.

"This neuron, like many others that we studied, supplies NE to a very large volume of the cerebral cortex. For the brain, this is highly unusual. Most neurons are more specific in their targets," noted Jeremiah Cohen, scientist at the Allen Institute and study co-author. "But this neuron doesn't release NE everywhere. It ignores the cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord.".

Despite its remarkable length and extensive reach, the neuron does not distribute norepinephrine throughout the entire brain. Instead, its connections remain selective, reinforcing the discovery that the LC operates through carefully organized signaling pathways.

A Latest Understanding of How the Brain Learns.

The researchers also identified intriguing similarities between the norepinephrine system and the brain's dopamine signaling system.

Dopamine is another major chemical messenger that sends signals to the basal ganglia, a brain region involved in forming habits. Scientists suspect that dopamine and norepinephrine work together to support learning, potentially allowing the brain to acquire several complex and abstract concepts at the same time.

By revealing the intricate connections, specialized functions, and unusual physical structure of neurons in the locus coeruleus, the research provides a more detailed picture of how the animal brain communicates and learns.

Although the findings come from experiments in mice, they could eventually help scientists better understand human brain function and design treatments that target specific neural circuits rather than affecting entire signaling systems.

Group biography follows Lee Miller, Pablo Picasso and friends on holiday in the South of France

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A group biography balances between a choir and a cacophony.
  • Industry observers note that the individuals gathered in the Hotel Vaste Horizon in the French village of Mougins formed the chain of couples constituting this community: Eileen Agar and Joseph Bard, Nusch and Paul Éluard, Ady Fidelin and Man Ray, Dora Maar and Pablo Picasso, Lee Miller and Roland Penrose.
  • According to recent reports, from this carefree and creative escape, Thomasson’s narrative plunges its participants into the war.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A group biography balances between a choir and a cacophony. Each person lies at the heart of a network, opening the potential for an exponential chain of many walk-on parts. Rooted in the photographs of what author Anna Thomasson rightly terms the “fleeting community” of a late summer holiday in 1937, A Vast Horizon succeeds remarkably in marshalling a complex tapestry of egos, events, ideals and disappointments.

Industry observers note that the individuals gathered in the Hotel Vaste Horizon in the French village of Mougins formed the chain of couples constituting this community: Eileen Agar and Joseph Bard, Nusch and Paul Éluard, Ady Fidelin and Man Ray, Dora Maar and Pablo Picasso, Lee Miller and Roland Penrose. They were drawn to the South of France by their inter-linked friendships and by “le peintre soleil”, Agar’s witty characterisation of Picasso. As Picasso urged everyone to work, half the witnesses took photographs. Maar, Man Ray and Miller were the relaxing professionals; snapshots were added by Agar and Penrose. Thomasson has searched through this rich, if scattered visual archive of a moment through which photography (as Roland Barthes recognised in Camera Lucida) “mechanically repeats what could never be repeated existentially”. Their hedonism caught in this moment defied the political instability and totalitarianism, with civil war already a year old in Spain.

According to recent reports, from this carefree and creative escape, Thomasson’s narrative plunges its participants into the war. For each of them it constituted a restructuring of values—not as hoped for by the Surrealists, but as enforced by the destructive triumphalism of Nazi extremism. Here the account turns to Paul Éluard’s transformation of a love poem for Nusch into a litany for “liberty” that captured the spirit of resistance (copies were even dropped over Occupied France by the RAF). Equally powerful was Miller’s reportage of the savagery of combat and, eventually, the revelations of the concentration camps. In this way, the book touches upon the transience of bodies captured in photography: those at Hotel Vaste Horizon were willingly posed for the camera and exchanged in partnerships, before growing fragile through wartime deprivation.

In a recent development, there was no reciprocal gathering in the post-war period. As a result, Thomasson traces the endgames, as each of the participants ages in varying degrees of dignity, creativity and despair. Those bodies displayed on the beach in southern France become the distant, optimistic opposite to the tragic, haunting corpses of Buchenwald; it is little wonder that Miller, the photographer in both cases, would never fully recover from the experience of witnessing such deliberate inhumanity.

Picnic of stars: Lee Miller’s 1937 photo of (left to right) Nusch and Paul Éluard, Roland Penrose, Man Ray and Ady Fidelin.

Recent findings suggest that while the lives of many of these central figures are, to varying degrees, familiar—from autobiographies (Agar, Man Ray, Penrose) and biographies (Éluard, Miller, Picasso)—Thomasson’s synthesis draws on recent research and extensive reading. A particular strength is the rebalancing of longstanding gender biases and assumptions. The repositioning of Ady Fidelin, the double-marginalised Guadeloupean woman, is especially timely; drawing on fresh scholarship, she is given greater presence and somewhat rescued from simply being Man Ray’s model. Nusch Éluard is also brought more sharply into focus. Substantial traces of these women’s own voices remain to be found, however, confining them to an unknowability ascribed to their devotion to their partners, although this may be overstated in the suggestion that, in 1946, Nusch Éluard “died in the service of Paul [Éluard]’s pursuit of freedom”.

Late on Thomasson cites Emily Dickinson’s belief that veracity is “more affecting, if told indirectly”. This emerges as a foundational conceit in a volume inspired by photographs but in which only four are reproduced. Instead of showing, the author presents often highly evocative descriptions of what she sees in a wide range of images that the reader is not shown. This is a surprising decision for a narrative stimulated, as we are told, by the author being drawn into “their distant world by their photographs”.

It has been revealed that with such a limitation on images, the book’s cover photograph assumes disproportionate significance. Where the British edition favours Agar’s photograph of Maar, Picasso and the Éluards at Juan-les-Pins, Miller’s picnic photograph of “half-naked women sitting among fully clothed men”—the jarring nature of which introduces the whole narrative—appears on the cover of the US edition. Although unaltered when reproduced inside the volume, on the cover the half-naked torsos are rather ineptly airbrushed. That the publishers chose to manipulate a famous 90-year-old image seems an unfortunate undermining of an otherwise compelling narrative of artists embracing freedom before disaster struck.

ª A Vast Horizon: Artists and Lovers, Freedom and War, by Anna Thomasson, published by Pegasus Books, 304pp, 4 b/w reproductions, $29.95 (hb), 7 July.

Latest Update: Breakthrough PTSD treatment achieves 68% remission rate in clinical trial

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1827 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced approach to treating post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) has received FDA clearance, offering a personalized alternative for people who have not found sufficient relief through existing treatments.
  • Early clinical trial findings have been encouraging.
  • The need for more effective PTSD care is substantial.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced approach to treating post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) has received FDA clearance, offering a personalized alternative for people who have not found sufficient relief through existing treatments. Developed by California-based Wave Neuroscience in collaboration with researchers at the Texas A&M Health Institute of Biosciences and Technology, the technology uses brain activity measurements to guide targeted magnetic stimulation.

Early clinical trial findings have been encouraging. According to Wave Neuroscience, patients experienced a 52% reduction in PTSD symptoms, while 68% achieved remission. The full findings are still being prepared for public release, but researchers believe the technology could significantly expand treatment options for millions of people.

The need for more effective PTSD care is substantial. In the United States, approximately 17.5 veterans die by suicide each day, and about 7% of veterans receive a PTSD diagnosis annually.

PTSD can develop after traumatic experiences such as military combat, serious accidents, natural disasters, or violence. An estimated 6% of Americans will experience PTSD during their lifetime, with higher rates among women and veterans.

Why Current PTSD Treatments Are Not Enough.

Since PTSD was formally recognized as a diagnosis in 1980, treatment has largely centered on psychotherapy and medications known as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), including sertraline and fluoxetine.

Although these approaches can help, many patients continue to experience symptoms despite receiving treatment.

It has been revealed that A 2020 review of PTSD medications found that patients reported improvements ranging from 6.8 to 10.1 points on symptom assessments. However, remission rates reached only 10.9% at most.

In a recent development, wave Neuroscience reported substantially stronger preliminary outcomes in its clinical trial. Erik Won, DO, the tech giant's chief medical officer, described the results as a major advance over previously reported medication outcomes.

Sources indicate that “In comparison to that study, our FDA trial reported a 52% reduction in symptoms, so more than a four-fold increase in efficacy,” Won said. “And more importantly, we saw 68% remission in our clinical trial. So, it’s really a quantum change, an inflection point in what we can offer to patients. From a clinical care perspective, that’s really meaningful.”.

These findings are promising, although the results come from different studies and should not be interpreted as a direct comparison of treatment effectiveness.

How Personalized Brain Stimulation Works.

The newly cleared system uses Magnetic e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT), a technology that combines measurements of brain activity with targeted magnetic stimulation.

First, an electroencephalogram (EEG) records the brain's electrical signals. This information helps guide a personalized treatment blueprint using transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS.

During TMS, a coil positioned against the scalp delivers magnetic pulses that stimulate brain activity. The technique has already been used for other psychiatric conditions, including treatment-resistant depression.

What distinguishes MeRT is its use of an AI-assisted algorithm to customize stimulation protocols based on each patient's brain activity rather than relying on a standardized approach.

“Transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, was previously FDA cleared for treatment-resistant depression,” Won mentioned. “By adding an augmented AI derived multivariate algorithm, we were able to personalize protocols that received FDA clearance for post-traumatic stress disorder, which should open up market access to about 13 million people who may be struggling with PTSD.”.

In a recent development, dr. Kenneth S. Ramos, a physician-scientist at Texas A&M Health with extensive experience in precision medicine, helped guide the research.

His work focuses on adapting medical care to the characteristics of individual patients instead of assuming that everyone will respond to the same treatment.

“Most clinical interventions for the treatment of PTSD do not work very well,” Ramos said. “So, this is a huge area where identifying interventions that could hopefully add quality of life to the people impacted by this disorder would be tremendously impactful.”.

Wave Neuroscience CEO Fred Walke said Ramos was a natural fit for the project because of his expertise in personalized medicine.

Targeting PTSD With Greater Precision.

Conventional TMS generally follows treatment protocols that are less individualized. MeRT builds on the same underlying technology but adjusts treatment according to the patient's specific brain activity.

Ramos emphasized that even small biological differences between people can have major implications for medical care. Humans are approximately 99.9% genetically alike, yet the remaining 0.1% contributes to differences that can influence how individuals respond to treatment.

By accounting for these differences and tailoring stimulation to each person's brain, researchers observed substantial reductions in PTSD symptom severity.

Ramos illustrated the distinction with an analogy involving a leaking roof.

He likened conventional TMS to covering a leak with a tarp to manage its effects. MeRT, in contrast, aims to provide a more targeted solution, comparable to identifying and replacing the damaged shingles responsible for the problem.

The broader goal is to move beyond treating patients with standardized protocols and toward interventions guided by measurable biological information.

From Breakthrough Designation to FDA Clearance.

The regulatory process reached an notable milestone in 2024, when MeRT received an FDA Breakthrough Device designation.

Industry observers note that dr. Rick Silva, executive director of clinical trials at the Texas A&M Health Institute of Biosciences and Technology, explained that the designation helps promising technologies move through regulatory review more efficiently.

It does not eliminate scientific or medical requirements. Instead, it can streamline communication and reduce administrative delays while preserving the standards needed for FDA clearance.

Silva noted the progress was particularly meaningful because the project began during the COVID-19 pandemic and advanced through the regulatory process unusually swiftly.

According to recent reports, according to Silva, medical device development and clinical evaluation can often take around 10 years before clearance is obtained. This project completed the relevant process in just over two years.

He credited the experience and dedication of the Wave Neuroscience team with helping make that accelerated progress possible.

It has been revealed that “I’ve been involved in probably close to 1,000 projects in academic medical centers over the years at varying degrees of depth and detail,” Silva noted. “Patients are why I do what I do. It’s hard, and the failure rate is high, and it’s a lot of work. But when you get to a point where something is going to benefit patients, it’s very professionally gratifying and personally gratifying in many ways as well.”.

A New Drug-Free Option for PTSD Patients.

Dr. Israel Liberzon, distinguished professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at the Texas A&M Naresh K. Vashisht College of Medicine, served as the study's lead psychiatrist and PTSD specialist.

He believes the clearance represents an important expansion of the available treatments for PTSD.

According to Liberzon, MeRT will become the only FDA-cleared nonmedication treatment specifically for PTSD once it reaches patients.

“Right now, the FDA has approved only two medications for PTSD,” Liberzon remarked. “It doesn’t mean that only two of them are used, but both are SSRIs. This is the first time that in addition to the medication, we have a non-medication option. There is psychotherapy that people use for PTSD, but psychotherapies require a lot of effort. People must participate actively, and many drop out because it’s too anxiety provoking. So now we have a unique alternative.”.

In the clinical trial, participants received five treatment sessions each week over a period of five to six weeks.

Researchers reported that the improvements appeared to persist after the treatment sessions ended, suggesting the benefits may extend beyond the active therapy period.

For patients who struggle with medication side effects or find psychotherapy difficult to complete, a treatment based on personalized brain stimulation could provide another option.

“People living with PTSD have been left with trial-and-error treatment, medications and their side effects, and limited outcomes—even when treated by the most dedicated and experienced physicians,” Won said. “Wave’s FDA clearance signals a fundamentally different future: one in which PTSD can be objectively evaluated, precisely treated and meaningfully healed.”.

Won also believes the technology could eventually be adapted to other psychiatric conditions, including depression and anxiety.

Could Personalized Brain Therapy Transform Mental Healthcare?

Recent findings suggest that dr. Leslie S. Prichep, chief scientific officer at Wave Neuroscience, sees the FDA clearance as an vital step toward treatment decisions guided by objective measurements of brain function.

“The FDA clearance of the MeRT System reflects decades of scientific research using electrophysiological biomarkers in identifying abnormal brain activity profiles and guiding personalized intervention strategies,” Prichep said. “We believe this represents an important advancement toward a more objective, data-informed model of mental healthcare.”.

Walke believes that giving patients clearer information about their brain activity could also help change public attitudes toward mental illness.

It has been revealed that he compared the idea to treating a broken bone with a cast. By making mental health conditions easier to understand through measurable physical information, the manufacturer hopes to reduce stigma and help patients better understand their experiences.

It has been revealed that “One of the goals of the company is to create a platform for mental healthcare that uses objective imagery to help patients understand why they’re experiencing life the way that they are,” Walke remarked. “That insight, compounded with proven technologies, promises incredibly high efficacy when personalized.”.

It has been revealed that an crucial next step will be ensuring that patients can actually obtain the treatment. Wave Neuroscience and Texas A&M Health are working with other stakeholders to expand availability and make the therapy more affordable through insurance coverage.

In a recent development, “Our hope is that this research and technology can be a catalyst for more widespread development and innovation of more effective, personalized and precision-guided treatments,” Won said. “This is proof positive that population-scale personalized medicine is not just an aspirational goal but is an achievable reality today.”.

The project combines years of work across medicine, neuroscience, clinical research, and technology, all directed toward improving the lives of people affected by PTSD.

For Ramos, the opportunity to help veterans carries particular significance because of Texas A&M's longstanding involvement in military and veteran initiatives.

According to recent reports, “Texas A&M has a very rich history of military and veteran priorities,” Ramos said. “It’s a no-brainer that Texas A&M faculty would be interested in and supportive of an initiative that hopefully would bring positive solutions to a major problem. And anything we could do to help alleviate that problem is going to go a long way towards making a difference in the individual’s life as well as the people who are close to them. I feel very fortunate that we at Texas A&M were meaningfully involved in this project.”.

#160563. Mediterranean diet may boost tiny proteins that protect the heart and brain

Mediterranean diet may boost tiny proteins that protect the heart and brain

📅 25 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1495 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced study suggests that the Mediterranean diet may protect the heart, brain, and aging cells through a surprising biological mechanism involving tiny proteins produced by mitochondria, the structures responsible for generating most of the energy our cells need.
  • Researchers at the USC Leonard Davis School of Gerontology discovered that people who more closely followed the Mediterranean diet had higher levels of two mitochondrial microproteins called humanin and SHMOOSE.
  • The study, led by USC Leonard Davis Instructional Associate Professor of Gerontology Roberto Vicinanza, offers a possible explanation for how everyday food choices influence cellular health and the aging process.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced study suggests that the Mediterranean diet may protect the heart, brain, and aging cells through a surprising biological mechanism involving tiny proteins produced by mitochondria, the structures responsible for generating most of the energy our cells need.

Researchers at the USC Leonard Davis School of Gerontology discovered that people who more closely followed the Mediterranean diet had higher levels of two mitochondrial microproteins called humanin and SHMOOSE. Both have previously been linked to protection against cardiovascular disease and neurodegeneration, the gradual deterioration of nerve cells that occurs in conditions such as Alzheimer's disease.

The study, led by USC Leonard Davis Instructional Associate Professor of Gerontology Roberto Vicinanza, offers a possible explanation for how everyday food choices influence cellular health and the aging process.

In a recent development, "These microproteins may act as molecular messengers that translate what we eat into how our cells function and age," Vicinanza remarked. "It's a newly introduced biological pathway that helps explain why the Mediterranean diet is so powerful.".

How the Mediterranean Diet May Protect Aging Cells.

The Mediterranean diet emphasizes foods such as olive oil, fish, beans, lentils, fruits, and vegetables. It has consistently been associated with a lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and cognitive decline. However, scientists are still working to understand exactly how this eating pattern produces its wide-ranging health benefits.

To investigate, the researchers examined blood samples from older adults who followed the Mediterranean diet to different degrees. Those whose eating habits most closely matched the diet had significantly higher concentrations of humanin and SHMOOSE.

They also showed lower indicators of oxidative stress, a process in which harmful molecules called reactive oxygen species overwhelm the body's protective defenses. Over time, oxidative stress can damage proteins, DNA, and other cellular components, contributing to aging and chronic disease.

It has been revealed that interestingly, the researchers found that certain foods were associated with different microproteins. Higher consumption of olive oil, fish, and legumes was linked to increased humanin levels. Meanwhile, olive oil consumption and eating fewer refined carbohydrates were associated with higher levels of SHMOOSE.

According to recent reports, refined carbohydrates include foods made with heavily processed grains and sugars, such as white bread, pastries, and many sugary snacks. These foods generally contain less fiber and fewer naturally occurring nutrients than their minimally processed counterparts.

"These findings suggest that specific components of the Mediterranean diet may directly influence mitochondrial biology," stated USC Leonard Davis School Dean and USC Distinguished Professor Pinchas Cohen, the study's senior author. "Humanin and SHMOOSE could serve as biomarkers for adherence to the Mediterranean diet and have clinical significance.".

Biomarkers are measurable biological indicators that can provide information about a person's health or physiological state. In this case, the researchers suggest that humanin and SHMOOSE could eventually help scientists understand how closely someone's diet aligns with healthy eating patterns and how their cells respond.

Tiny Mitochondrial Proteins With Powerful Effects.

Industry observers note that the findings extend a scientific effort spanning more than 20 years to investigate small proteins produced by mitochondria. Cohen has played a leading role in discovering and studying these molecules, which are increasingly recognized as vital participants in cellular health.

Mitochondria are often described as the powerhouses of cells because they produce much of the energy required for essential biological activities. But their role extends beyond energy production. They also help regulate metabolism, cellular stress responses, and processes associated with aging.

Unlike most proteins, which are produced using instructions stored in the DNA inside the cell's nucleus, mitochondrial microproteins originate from genetic instructions within mitochondria themselves.

These instructions are found in small segments of mitochondrial DNA known as open reading frames. Some of these regions were once considered nonfunctional, but researchers have discovered that they can encode biologically active molecules.

According to recent reports, one of the best understood is humanin, first identified by Cohen and fellow researchers in 2003. Subsequent studies have associated humanin with improved insulin sensitivity, better cardiovascular health, increased longevity, and protection of cognitive abilities.

Insulin sensitivity refers to how effectively the body's cells respond to insulin, the hormone that helps regulate blood sugar. Maintaining healthy insulin sensitivity is key for metabolic health and reducing the risk of type 2 diabetes.

Another intriguing microprotein is SHMOOSE (Small Human Mitochondrial ORF Over SErine tRNA), which was identified more recently by Cohen's research team.

It has been revealed that SHMOOSE has attracted particular interest because of its possible role in protecting the brain. Scientists have found that a genetic variant of SHMOOSE is associated with an increased risk of Alzheimer's disease. The normal version, meanwhile, appears to help protect neurons from damage involving amyloid, a protein that can accumulate abnormally in the brains of people with Alzheimer's.

In a recent development, "These peptides are emerging as key regulators of aging biology," Cohen said. "They connect mitochondrial function to diseases like Alzheimer's and heart disease and now, potentially, to nutrition.".

A Hidden Mechanism for Protecting the Heart.

The scientists also identified a potentially notable connection between humanin and an enzyme called Nox2, which helps generate reactive oxygen species.

Although these molecules have useful roles in normal cell signaling and immune defense, excessive production can contribute to oxidative stress and damage blood vessels and other tissues.

The researchers observed that people with higher humanin levels tended to have lower Nox2 activity. This relationship raises the possibility that humanin helps limit damaging oxidative processes, potentially offering an additional layer of cardiovascular protection.

Sources indicate that based on these findings, the researchers propose that the Mediterranean diet could support heart health in two complementary ways. The diet may help reduce oxidative stress directly while also supporting the production of mitochondrial microproteins that influence pathways involved in cellular damage.

However, the observed associations do not establish that the diet directly increases these proteins or that the proteins themselves prevent cardiovascular disease.

"This could represent a new cardioprotective mechanism of the Mediterranean diet," Vicinanza noted.

Bringing the Mediterranean Diet to a Global Audience.

Vicinanza's interest in the Mediterranean diet extends beyond investigating its effects inside the body. He has also worked to promote this traditional eating pattern internationally as a way to support human health, cultural heritage, and environmental sustainability.

As part of those efforts, he collaborated with the Municipality of Pollica in Italy, which is recognized as a UNESCO Mediterranean Diet emblematic community.

That collaboration helped support the establishment of the International Day of the Mediterranean Diet through the United Nations.

Observed every year on November 16, the international event is intended to draw attention to the Mediterranean diet's health benefits as well as its cultural traditions and environmental significance.

For Vicinanza, the upcoming findings reinforce the relationship between traditional food practices and modern discoveries about how the body functions.

Industry observers note that "We're connecting centuries-old dietary traditions with cutting-edge molecular biology," Vicinanza said. "It supports the idea that healthy eating patterns with little to no ultra-processed foods reflect how humans have eaten over long periods and may create conditions to which mitochondria -- ancient cellular organelles -- are likely adapted.".

Could Tiny Proteins Help Unlock Healthier Aging?

Recent findings suggest that although the findings are promising, the researchers emphasize that the study was relatively small and observational. That means it identified relationships between dietary habits and biological measurements but could not determine whether eating a Mediterranean diet directly caused the differences in microprotein levels.

Other factors, including participants' overall health and lifestyle, could also influence the results.

Nevertheless, the discovery opens an intriguing possibility for the emerging field of precision nutrition, which seeks to develop dietary recommendations based on an individual's biological characteristics and needs.

If future research confirms that dietary changes can reliably influence humanin, SHMOOSE, and related microproteins, these molecules could potentially become useful tools for evaluating nutritional interventions and developing more personalized strategies for healthy aging.

The next step is to determine whether adopting a Mediterranean-style diet actually increases these proteins and whether those changes lead to measurable improvements in cardiovascular health, brain function, or disease risk.

Recent findings suggest that "Our goal is to move from observing associations to understanding causality," Vicinanza stated. "If we can harness these pathways, we may be able to design nutritional strategies that promote healthy aging at the molecular level.".

The work was funded by the USC Daryl and Irwin Simon Nutrition for Alzheimer's Disease Prevention Research Fund (to Vicinanza), the Hanson-Thorell Family Research Award (to Vicinanza), National Institutes of Health grant P30AG094848 (to Cohen) and PRIN 2022 grant 000031_23_PP_PIGNATELLI_PRIN_2022-B53D23021240006 (to Pignatelli).

#160562. Are Chimps Less Likely to Steal From Friends?

Are Chimps Less Likely to Steal From Friends?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (768 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In recent years, scientists have shown that chimpanzees favor certain peers by picking whom they prefer to groom and selectively sharing food.
  • But a question has lingered: How might a chimpanzee friendship affect antisocial acts?
  • It has been revealed that in a new study that uses fruit as the loot, UC Berkeley researchers found that chimps steal less from their friends, and that friendship status affected the emotional expression of both victim and thieves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In recent years, scientists have shown that chimpanzees favor certain peers by picking whom they prefer to groom and selectively sharing food. The behavior offers a glimpse into humanity’s prosocial evolutionary past.

But a question has lingered: How might a chimpanzee friendship affect antisocial acts?

It has been revealed that in a new study that uses fruit as the loot, UC Berkeley researchers found that chimps steal less from their friends, and that friendship status affected the emotional expression of both victim and thieves. Closely bonded chimps swiped pineapple pieces from one another less frequently than those with weaker relationships. Additionally, victims were quicker to calm down when the thief was a friend, and thieves highlighted less hostility when stealing from a bonded pal than from a non-friend.

The new research deepens our understanding of the emotional underpinnings of our social lives, said Oded Ritov, the paper’s first author and a Berkeley psychology Ph.D. student.

In a recent development, “Collaborative relationships are notable for our well-being, health, and survival,” said Ritov, who works with Berkeley’s Social Origins Lab. “Increasingly, we’re understanding that this isn’t something that’s unique to us, but that other animals have friends, as well.”.

The paper was published online in September and will appear in the November issue of the journal Evolution and Human Behavior.

Industry observers note that scientists are sometimes hesitant to describe an apparently close relationship between chimps as akin to human friendship, arguing that we can’t grasp their cognitive and emotional complexity. To identify those who revealed signs of a close relationship, researchers observed 26 chimps for more than 800 hours at the Ngamba Island Chimpanzee Sanctuary in Uganda. The team documented which chimps appeared to be closely bonded—like friends—by taking note of their grooming patterns, daily interactions, and how regularly they were within arm’s reach of others.

According to recent reports, then they set up two rooms. One contained a “victim” chimp with three trays baited with pineapple. Researchers attached a rope to the trays and led it into the other room, where a second chimp—the thief—could either leave the rope alone or yank it to steal the pineapple.

Chimps stole in 70% of trials with non-friends, compared with 61% of trials with friends. While 9 percentage points may not seem large, each chimp experienced both friend and non-friend conditions, a methodological technique that leads to a higher degree of confidence that the difference is meaningful and not just random chance.

“Ours is the first study to show that they’re able to hold back antisocial behavior with their friends,” Ritov mentioned.

According to recent reports, researchers also measured how the victims responded to being stolen from by evaluating their stomping, fist-pounding, and screeching. Victims were initially angrier when friends stole from them but quickly moderated their feelings compared with when non-friends stole from them.

The thieves’ behavior also changed. When non-friends were the thieves, the thieves expressed negative emotions for much longer, suggesting they viewed the interaction as more hostile.

“This suggests that there may be mutual expectations in chimps from both sides of the friendship, which makes it seem more like the complex friendships we see in humans,” Ritov said.

Recent findings suggest that jan Engelmann, an associate professor of psychology and principal investigator with the Social Origins Lab, said previous work has shown relationship-specific intentions in nonhuman primates. But human friendships are about more than special intentions, he added—they’re about stronger expectations.

In a recent development, “We expect more of our friends,” mentioned Engelmann, a senior author of the paper. “These findings really deepen our understanding of the evolutionary roots of friendships. This is, to my knowledge, the first evidence showing that also chimpanzees expect and maybe demand special treatment from their friends. These kinds of social expectations might form the basis of human moral principles.”.

The paper adds to Ritov’s work that focuses on the evolution of human behavior and how morals and norms are part of our core being, traceable to other animals. He has recently studied whether nonhuman animals have a sense of fairness and is broadly interested in how emotions unfold across cultures and species.

“We think that these expectations might be the basic building blocks of the larger-scale cooperation we see in humans,” Ritov said. “The expectations that chimpanzees have from their friends or close collaborative partners might have scaled up to more generalized expectations for how we should treat each other.”.

This article was originally published on Berkeley News. Read the original article.

Jason Pohl is a science writer in UC Berkeley's Office of Communications & Public Affairs.

#160561. This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans

📅 25 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1720 w)

This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans

📅 25 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1720 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, people living thousands of miles apart have reported an extraordinarily strange experience after eating certain wild mushrooms.
  • In a recent development, these visions are known as Lilliputian hallucinations, named after the miniature inhabitants of "Gulliver's Travels," who stand just 6 inches tall.
  • Now, a new study provides evidence that the phenomenon has a biological explanation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, people living thousands of miles apart have reported an extraordinarily strange experience after eating certain wild mushrooms. They begin seeing tiny human figures that appear to move through the real world, walking around objects, climbing over surfaces, and interacting with their surroundings.

In a recent development, these visions are known as Lilliputian hallucinations, named after the miniature inhabitants of "Gulliver's Travels," who stand just 6 inches tall. For decades, researchers suspected that cultural beliefs and folklore might explain why people in different regions described such similar experiences.

Now, a new study provides evidence that the phenomenon has a biological explanation.

Researchers at the University of Utah (U) used DNA sequencing to identify Lanmaoa asiatica as the mushroom responsible for these unusual hallucinations in Southwest China and the northern Philippines. Surprisingly, their investigation found no evidence of any known psychoactive mushroom compounds, including psilocybin.

According to recent reports, the findings suggest that the mushroom may produce an entirely unfamiliar hallucinogenic substance. Identifying that chemical could help scientists better understand neurological disorders, unusual visual experiences, and the processes through which the brain creates our perception of reality.

Sources indicate that the research was conducted by Colin Domnauer, a doctoral student at the U, and Bryn Dentinger, a mycologist affiliated with the university and the Natural History Museum of Utah. Their findings were published in the journal Mycologia.

In an interview with @theU, Domnauer explained how researchers traced the mushroom's identity, what makes its effects so unusual, and why the discovery could have implications far beyond the study of fungi.

A Century-Old Mystery of Tiny Human Hallucinations.

The scientific mystery dates back to 1934, when Western researchers learned that people in Papua Latest Guinea sometimes experienced vivid visions of miniature humans after eating wild mushrooms. The bizarre effect became known as "mushroom madness.".

It has been revealed that during the 1950s and 1960s, anthropologists and mushroom specialists traveled to Papua New Guinea to investigate. Their work pointed toward several possible species belonging to the Boletaceae (bolete) family.

According to recent reports, however, chemical testing failed to reveal any substances that could explain the hallucinations. Samples were even examined by Albert Hofmann, the scientist who first isolated psilocybin and discovered LSD. He, too, was unable to identify an active ingredient.

Recent findings suggest that with no chemical explanation available, some researchers began questioning whether the mushrooms were responsible at all. They suggested that the visions might instead arise from cultural expectations or traditional beliefs. By the end of the 1960s, scientific investigation of the phenomenon had largely stopped.

It has been revealed that the mystery resurfaced during the 1990s, when people in Yunnan, Southwest China, reported similar hallucinations after eating bolete mushrooms. Although the precise species remained uncertain, researchers suspected a recently described mushroom called Lanmaoa asiatica.

Scientists Identify the Mushroom Behind the Strange Visions.

Another crucial clue appeared in 2024, when Domnauer learned of comparable experiences among an Indigenous community in the remote Northern Cordillera region of the Philippines.

Community members described a wild edible mushroom called "Sedesdem" that could sometimes cause people to see miniature human figures. Similar mushrooms were known locally as "Nonda" in Papua Fresh Guinea and "Jian shou qing" in Yunnan.

These mushrooms have an crucial place in local food traditions, but consuming them without thoroughly cooking them can trigger the unusual hallucinations.

The Philippine accounts represented a third independent report of wild mushrooms causing remarkably similar visions of tiny people.

To investigate, Domnauer traveled to Yunnan and the Philippines, interviewed local residents, and collected specimens of L. asiatica along with other mushrooms belonging to the Lanmaoa genus.

Sources indicate that the fieldwork included the first scientific survey of fungi in the northern Philippines. Researchers then analyzed DNA from the collected mushrooms to establish their identities and evolutionary relationships.

It has been revealed that the results revealed that the mushrooms called Jian shou qing in China and Sedesdem in the Philippines were both L. asiatica.

This was an unexpected finding because scientists had previously believed the species occurred only in China.

Dentinger also visited Papua Upcoming Guinea in hopes of collecting specimens from the location where the mystery originally began. Unfortunately, unusually dry weather made it impossible to obtain samples for genetic comparison.

Although the Papua New Guinea mushroom remains unverified, the evidence from China and the Philippines provides a compelling connection. Three geographically separated cultures have described the same highly specific hallucinations, and DNA testing has linked two of those cases to a single mushroom species.

That consistency strongly suggests a shared chemical and neurological explanation rather than unrelated cultural influences.

Hallucinations of Tiny Humans That Seem Remarkably Real.

What makes these hallucinations especially unusual is their striking similarity across different accounts.

Sources indicate that people typically describe seeing dozens or even hundreds of miniature figures, generally measuring between 3 and 30 centimeters tall. The figures appear with extraordinary clarity, often seeming as solid and convincing as actual people.

According to Domnauer, approximately 90% of those experiencing the visions describe figures resembling elves, clowns, or other fairy-like characters, often wearing brightly colored clothing.

Even more surprising is the way these imaginary figures seem to behave.

Rather than floating through walls or ignoring their surroundings, they appear to follow familiar physical rules. They walk around obstacles, move across ordinary objects, and sometimes tumble from the edges of tables.

Sources indicate that domnauer recalled one particularly unusual account involving someone eating soup. The person reported seeing tiny humans leap from a spoon into the bowl, where they began swimming. When the person took another spoonful, the miniature figures reportedly remained visible inside their mouth.

Such detailed interactions distinguish these visions from many other forms of drug-induced hallucination.

A Mysterious Psychedelic Compound Unlike Any Known Drug.

Scientists also investigated whether L. asiatica contains any of the chemicals already known to cause psychedelic experiences.

Using both chemical testing and genetic analysis, the researchers searched for established psychoactive compounds found in other mushroom species.

The absence of familiar hallucinogens was particularly intriguing because the mushroom's effects differ so dramatically from those associated with known psychedelic drugs.

Researchers now suspect that L. asiatica produces an unidentified psychoactive substance responsible for the tiny human hallucinations.

The compound has not yet been isolated or chemically identified, so its exact nature and mechanism remain unknown.

Discovering it could open an entirely newly introduced avenue of research into how certain chemicals alter visual perception.

What the Mushroom Could Reveal About the Human Brain.

Although L. asiatica provides an unusually consistent trigger for Lilliputian hallucinations, the phenomenon is not limited to mushroom consumption.

In a recent development, stories involving miniature humanlike beings appear throughout folklore around the world. Similar hallucinations have also been documented in people experiencing alcohol withdrawal, dementia, macular degeneration, and other neurological conditions.

These connections suggest that the visions may arise from a fundamental feature of the way the human brain processes visual information.

However, scientists still do not fully understand the neurological mechanisms responsible for these experiences or how best to treat them when they occur in medical settings.

This is where the mysterious mushroom could become especially valuable.

Sources indicate that unlike the neurological and medical conditions in which Lilliputian hallucinations occur relatively rarely, L. asiatica can produce the phenomenon in a more consistent and recognizable way.

If researchers can isolate the chemical responsible, they may gain a useful tool for investigating the brain circuits and processes that create these unusually detailed visual experiences.

Such research could eventually improve scientific understanding of hallucinations associated with neurological diseases.

The research team's next major objective is to isolate and identify the suspected psychedelic compound.

DNA Sequencing Reveals Four Previously Unknown Mushroom Species.

The investigation also produced important discoveries about fungal biodiversity.

Rather than studying L. asiatica alone, Domnauer and Dentinger conducted the first comprehensive genomic analysis of the Lanmaoa genus.

They examined 53 mushroom specimens collected from natural habitats and preserved in fungarium collections around the world.

Genetic sequencing revealed 17 species within the group, including four species previously unknown to science.

Sources indicate that remarkably, two of those newly identified species had already been preserved in existing collections in the United States. Their distinct identities had gone unrecognized until researchers examined their DNA.

According to recent reports, the analysis also indicated that L. asiatica is the only species in the genus at the moment known to produce psychoactive effects.

Sources indicate that scientists are now working to reconstruct the group's evolutionary history. They hope to determine how the unusual chemical trait developed and whether closely related mushrooms might produce comparable substances.

The findings also demonstrate the scientific value of museum collections. Specimens preserved for years can contain biological discoveries that become apparent only when newer analytical techniques are applied.

For Domnauer, the hidden diversity found in these collections is a reminder that many species and potentially important biological characteristics remain undiscovered, even among organisms that scientists have already collected.

Exploring Fungi Could Lead to Latest Medicines and Discoveries.

The broader implications extend well beyond unusual hallucinations.

Fungi remain one of the least thoroughly explored groups of organisms, and researchers believe their chemical diversity could provide valuable clues about biology, medicine, and the nervous system.

One of the most famous examples is penicillin, the antibiotic originally obtained from a fungus that transformed the treatment of bacterial infections and became one of the most consequential medical discoveries of the last century.

Scientists hope continued exploration of fungal biodiversity could reveal other medically useful compounds and previously unknown biological processes.

The mysterious effects of L. asiatica illustrate just how much remains to be learned about the fungal kingdom. A mushroom long consumed by communities in Asia may contain a substance capable of revealing fresh information about the human brain and how it creates conscious experience.

The research received funding from the National Science Foundation (award #DEB-2114785).

#160560. Breaking: How Artificial Intelligence Can Help With Critical Thinking

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (803 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: How Artificial Intelligence Can Help With Critical Thinking

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that knowledge workers such as scientists, teachers, lawyers, and business leaders are increasingly using generative artificial intelligence applications for tasks that demand imagination, creativity, and problem solving.
  • Scholars refer to this increasingly prevalent problem as cognitive offloading.
  • In a recent development, my research at the intersection of artificial intelligence and knowledge work provides a different view, however.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that knowledge workers such as scientists, teachers, lawyers, and business leaders are increasingly using generative artificial intelligence applications for tasks that demand imagination, creativity, and problem solving. Ironically, perhaps, recent research shows that people who interact with generative AI for work tasks can end up not thinking critically. They can surrender to AI’s quick and confident answers, which can lead to speedy but low-quality solutions.

Scholars refer to this increasingly prevalent problem as cognitive offloading. And they are showing that it can erode the very skills that make knowledge workers valuable.

In a recent development, my research at the intersection of artificial intelligence and knowledge work provides a different view, however. In one study, my colleagues and I interviewed 45 knowledge workers at a U.S. public university. They all were using generative AI applications in their core tasks: generating fresh ideas, solving complex problems, and designing novel solutions. We also analyzed the prompts and outputs from their iterative AI chats.

Industry observers note that we found that when knowledge workers intentionally use AI to challenge their ideas—to generate friction—they can significantly improve their performance. Previous research on human-AI collaboration for loan evaluations had similar results.

Using AI to find information that contradicts your own can reveal unlikely perspectives that disrupt your familiar logic and spark newly introduced insights. This is particularly key because AI models promptly become familiar with how a user prompts the model and interprets its output, and the model presents information according to these patterns.

For example, a marketing professional in our study asked AI to create virtual customers with personas that would lead them to dislike a product under development, which was an accounting certificate program. The contrary feedback from the AI model revealed customer preferences that the accounting professional designing the program had not considered, such as using multiple cases from different industries to illustrate a principle, rather than cases from the same industry.

In a recent development, an attorney used AI to find obscure legal loopholes and to consider how companies might exploit them. That exposed surprising but realistic scenarios of hard-to-detect unethical behavior in employees.

Exploring unlikely and opposing ideas presented by AI can feel disorienting. To help, knowledge workers should lean on their own expertise to question surprising information that an AI system might provide.

An operations research scientist who works with supply chains described adapting unfamiliar computing programs from other fields suggested by AI, such as signal processing and wireless communication, which helped him create a stronger program of his own. Although the programs were latest to him, his strong understanding of supply network modeling helped him see how he could apply them.

A study I was not involved with found that creative writers produce better copy when they use AI as a sounding board rather than to ghostwrite.

Knowledge workers can also use AI’s outputs to examine topics from multiple viewpoints, deepening their knowledge.

In a recent development, A research scholar in our study probed an AI system for journal papers that used a concept he was using, but in contrasting settings, which helped him understand the concept from different angles. A lawyer followed up on legal citations suggested by an AI model by asking for different types of illustrative cases. That helped her fully understand the original case and write a strong legal brief.

Leaders of organizations can encourage knowledge workers to develop friction-generating queries of AI models.

A straightforward approach is to use prompts that challenge rather than agree with a person’s thinking. People can also draw on their own knowledge, work experiences, and professional ethics to scrutinize AI outputs. Sometimes people realize that a response lacks originality, even if it is factually correct.

Organization leaders can also create programs for knowledge workers to share their experiences and insights. Regular sessions—led by cross-functional AI task forces or AI champions—can also help knowledge workers keep up with rapidly evolving AI tools.

In a recent development, providing resources for knowledge workers is important, as well. Internal AI bootcamps and workshops led by AI experts or experienced users can help workers understand what AI tools can and cannot do.

A professor leading an initiative about AI use in teaching described how she developed internal competitions with prizes for professors who successfully completed AI bootcamps. Organizations can also offer AI sandboxes—safe, private environments where employees can experiment and learn how to use AI tools.

In these efforts to support knowledge workers, an vital detail is pointing out that adding friction can appear to make an AI system work against you, but—as new research indicates—it actually helps it work for you.

Monideepa Tarafdar, Ph.D., is professor of information systems at UMass Amherst.

#160558. The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought

📅 28 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1294 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1294 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A major new study has uncovered crucial differences in how the brains of autistic children respond to human faces.
  • According to recent reports, some autistic people tend to look at faces less frequently or make less eye contact.
  • In a recent development, james McPartland, PhD, Harris Professor in the Child Study Center and director of the Center for Brain and Mind Health, studies how autistic people process faces using electroencephalography (EEG), a technique that records the brain's electrical activity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A major new study has uncovered crucial differences in how the brains of autistic children respond to human faces. Published in Nature Mental Health, the research is among the most extensive investigations yet into how face perception works in autism.

According to recent reports, some autistic people tend to look at faces less frequently or make less eye contact. They may also find it more difficult to remember faces or interpret facial expressions compared with neurotypical individuals. Scientists have spent decades investigating the brain activity behind these differences. In the early 2000s, for example, researchers at Yale reported that brain regions responsible for processing faces highlighted lower activity in autistic individuals than in people without autism.

In a recent development, james McPartland, PhD, Harris Professor in the Child Study Center and director of the Center for Brain and Mind Health, studies how autistic people process faces using electroencephalography (EEG), a technique that records the brain's electrical activity. Previous EEG studies, however, have typically examined signals from limited regions rather than analyzing activity across the entire scalp.

To gain a more complete picture, McPartland and his colleagues conducted a study involving approximately 400 autistic children, examining electrical signals recorded across the scalp. They discovered that brain activity associated with face recognition was less clearly distinguishable in autistic participants. They also identified a striking difference in development: In neurotypical children, the brain's response to faces became more specialized with age, while autistic children did not show the same pattern.

"This is the first time we've leveraged the full volume of very rich information provided by an EEG recording to understand face perception and autism," McPartland says.

How Scientists Discovered Differences in Autistic Brain Activity.

McPartland compares traditional approaches to studying face recognition with attempting to understand traffic throughout an entire city by monitoring just one downtown street.

"That's the way most research on face processing so far has worked," McPartland states.

The new approach provides a much broader perspective, similar to observing traffic across an entire city using satellite imagery. To investigate these patterns, the researchers analyzed information collected through the Autism Biomarkers Consortium for Clinical Trials (ABC-CT). The dataset included autistic and neurotypical children across different age groups.

According to recent reports, during the experiments, participants viewed pictures of faces and everyday objects while EEG equipment recorded their brain activity. Instead of concentrating on a small number of recording locations, the scientists examined electrical signals from all 128 electrodes positioned around each participant's scalp.

They then applied machine learning techniques to determine whether patterns in the recordings could reveal what each child was viewing.

The results showed that brain activity provided a clearer indication of face viewing in neurotypical children than in autistic children. In other words, the electrical signals associated with seeing faces were less distinguishable in the autistic group.

Recent findings suggest that "The neural activity that we measure at the scalp is just not as distinct in autistic children," notes first author Jason Griffin, PhD, assistant professor of psychology at University of Houston. Griffin previously worked as a postdoctoral researcher in McPartland's laboratory.

Industry observers note that the researchers also found that the ability to identify what a child was viewing from brain activity improved with age among neurotypical participants. This age related improvement was not observed in autistic children, suggesting that their neural responses to faces develop along a different pattern.

"Their face-specific processing is not following the same trajectory," Griffin says.

Face Recognition Differences May Begin Earlier Than Previously Thought.

Beyond identifying differences in brain activity, the study offers latest insight into how early those differences emerge during face perception.

Industry observers note that recognizing someone involves multiple stages of neural processing. The sequence begins when visual information enters the eyes and continues as the brain interprets that information until a face is recognized.

Much of the earlier research on autism and face perception has concentrated on a brain signal called the N170. This measurable change in electrical activity typically occurs about 170 milliseconds after a person sees a face. Previous studies have shown that the N170 response tends to occur later in autistic individuals.

By analyzing brain activity over a wider period, the researchers found evidence that differences in face processing begin before this familiar signal appears. This suggests that autism related differences may arise at earlier stages of visual processing than researchers had previously established.

"But when you look at face processing through an approach that's more inclusive of the full temporal range of information, we're seeing that differences in autism occur even earlier," McPartland says.

What the Discovery Could Mean for Autism Diagnosis and Early Support.

The findings could eventually influence how researchers approach autism diagnosis and the development of supportive interventions.

Historically, some clinicians attempted to address difficulties with face perception by requiring autistic individuals to maintain eye contact. Research has since shown that forcing eye contact is not an effective solution. A better understanding of how face processing develops in the brain could help identify approaches that are more useful and appropriate.

An ongoing challenge in autism research is separating neurological differences associated with autism itself from changes that may develop through the experience of living with the condition. According to the researchers, the patterns identified in this study suggest that differences in face processing are connected to underlying developmental characteristics of autism rather than simply reflecting accumulated life experiences.

"When we're seeing this expected refinement and specialization in non-autistic people, we're seeing a reduced developmental change in autistic people," McPartland explains.

Because the differences appear during development, the findings also raise the possibility that support aimed at helping autistic children interpret facial emotions could be particularly beneficial when introduced earlier in childhood.

However, the researchers emphasize that autism does not necessarily create difficulties that require intervention. Many neurodivergent people experience little or no impairment related to their autism and may neither need nor want additional support. For others, challenges with recognizing faces or understanding facial expressions can complicate everyday social interactions.

"Imagine navigating life when it's hard for you to perceive the information in another person's face, from navigating a playground to navigating a job interview," McPartland claims. "This is one of the critical areas that causes difficulty for many autistic people.".

New Brain Signals Could Help Improve Autism Diagnosis.

Another potential application involves the search for more objective ways to assess autism. Presently, clinicians diagnose autism primarily by evaluating behavior because reliable biological tests are not yet available for routine diagnosis.

Scientists are investigating several possible biomarkers, which are measurable biological characteristics that could improve diagnostic assessments or help distinguish different groups within the autism spectrum.

According to recent reports, the newly identified patterns of face related brain activity could contribute to that effort. By examining how these neural signals differ among individuals, researchers may eventually develop additional diagnostic tools or better identify autistic people who are likely to benefit from particular forms of support, including social skills therapy.

Although more research is necessary before these findings can be used in clinical practice, the study provides a new way to investigate how the autistic brain processes faces and how those responses change throughout childhood.

"This is a first step in introducing a fresh biomarker," McPartland states.

Latest Update: AI helps conservators uncover lost details in William Merritt Chase painting

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When William Merritt Chase’s painting A Comfortable Corner (around 1888) entered the conservation studio, the painting was carrying more than a century of history on its surface—including the interventions of conservators who had treated it decades earlier.
  • The newly restored painting, which is part of the collection of the Parrish Art Museum in Water Mill, New York, will be on display in its exhibition William Merritt Chase and Walter Granville-Smith: American Impressionists of the East End (14 November-21 March 2027).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When William Merritt Chase’s painting A Comfortable Corner (around 1888) entered the conservation studio, the painting was carrying more than a century of history on its surface—including the interventions of conservators who had treated it decades earlier. Artificial intelligence (AI) contributed to a restoration endeavour that has peeled back some of those interventions.

The newly restored painting, which is part of the collection of the Parrish Art Museum in Water Mill, New York, will be on display in its exhibition William Merritt Chase and Walter Granville-Smith: American Impressionists of the East End (14 November-21 March 2027). The Parrish has an especially deep connection to Chase, who was not only a prominent figure in Gilded Age New York but also spent time on Long Island’s East End, where the museum is located. Today, the Parrish holds a substantial body of Chase’s work, alongside archival material donated by the artist’s family.

A Comfortable Corner depicts a woman reclining in an elaborately furnished interior, dressed in a deep blue kimono and holding an uchiwa fan.“A Comfortable Corner is an key work within William Merritt Chase’s oeuvre as it depicts a specific moment in 19th-century art and Chase’s own period with influences of art and design from Japan,” indicates Kaitlin Halloran, the museum’s associate curator.

Over the years, at least two restorations substantially altered the appearance of the painting, including a significant effort in the 1960s. Among the changes made were the addition of a heavyweight, almost burlap-like lining, retouching and blotchy inpainting, and the use of uneven varnishes. Some of these interventions changed the surface texture of various areas or discoloured over time. Working with conservator Suzanne Siano and her team at Modern Art Conservation, the museum set out to determine what restoration was needed to get the painting ready for the exhibition.

In a recent development, A crucial piece of evidence to guide this process arrived in the form of an early photograph of the painting. The black-and-white image, understood to have been taken before the 1960s restoration, revealed that more of the composition had once been visible than what had survived in the painting. The work had apparently been reduced in size during the 1960s restoration, perhaps to fit a new stretcher or because damaged edges were folded over and effectively removed.

Conservators from Modern Art Conservation with William Merritt Chase's A Comfortable Corner (The Blue Kimono) (around 1888) Photo: Lindsey Del Rio for Modern Art Conservation.

It has been revealed that the photograph also revealed details in the composition that had disappeared. A curl of hair beneath the sitter’s ear was missing; parts of a decorative screen had become faint or vanished; and some delicate passages had been overpainted with heavier marks. The conservation team also found evidence of pentimenti—changes made by Chase himself—that were not apparent in the earlier photograph, adding another layer of complexity.

Industry observers note that “It is difficult to establish whether all of these changes resulted from earlier conservation,” Siano tells The Art Newspaper. “Some of it may have stemmed from a misreading of what the conservator was seeing. They may have been cleaning toward what they believed to be the original surface when, in fact, some of what they removed may have been changes or additions made by the artist.”.

Using AI, the historical photograph was combined with a colour image of the painting to create a composite showing areas where the two diverged.

Recent findings suggest that “Although we are reasonably adept with Photoshop, we felt it was worth seeing what AI could offer,” Siano notes. “It proved very helpful, largely because of its speed. It was not instantaneous, but it was considerably faster than assembling the comparison manually.”.

According to recent reports, the resulting image helped the team identify areas that warranted closer examination. One important discovery concerned Chase’s signature, which had become extremely faint, with some of its letters apparently covered by overpaint. Because Chase’s signature is relatively abstract, Siano believes it may have been mistaken for part of the carpet pattern during the earlier restoration.

The project, supported by a Bank of America grant, illustrates both the possibilities and the limitations of AI in conservation. “Tasks that once took considerable time can be completed more swiftly, and AI can provide additional information for us to weigh,” Siano claims. “Ultimately, however, conservation is carried out by a highly skilled individual or team, and we do not expect that to change.”.

In a recent development, siano stresses that they did not simply reinstate every discrepancy identified by the software. The historical photograph was neither high-resolution nor necessarily a record of the painting’s earliest state. Instead, the information the photograph provided was assessed alongside magnified examination, ultraviolet imaging, knowledge of Chase’s materials, and comparison with his other works.

Sources indicate that “Conservation is a combination of science, art history, craft, manual skill and artistry,” Siano claims. “AI is none of those things.”.

In a recent development, the Chase painting was the first time Siano’s studio had used AI as an aid in the conservation of a painting. “In terms of determining how to conserve a painting, we think AI’s use will remain very case-specific. We do expect it to become increasingly valuable as a research tool, however: for example, in helping to locate historical images or relevant source material.”.

Ultimately, Siano says, “the judgments conservators make are nuanced and subtle, and we doubt those qualities can be replicated by a machine”.

In a recent development, that three-column grid holds steady across every country section, from Belgium and Canada to China, Austria, and Hungary. #160555. Breaking: What My Son Is Learning From Artificial Intelligence
